title: Caption and prose channels select different argument arity on one diagram page
summary: GDT213 documents a readable medical page combining component captions with longer practical prose. A speculative functional hypothesis is that short caption units and prose units use different argument arity, rather than every token belonging to one homogeneous lexical channel.

design.unit: complete short caption or prose unit on a connected diagram page
design.contrast: caption channel has component/edge argument while prose channel has multi-step action arguments versus one shared lexical grammar
design.prediction: After fixing channel membership independently, caption units should show bounded component/edge argument slots and prose units should show longer action/participant sequences; cross-channel transfer should fail at the arity boundary.
design.countermodel: The visual distinction may be editorial formatting only, with one grammar producing both short and long units.
design.falsifier: Held caption and prose units have the same independently coded argument arity and transition behavior after page and register controls.
design.principal_risk: The comparator establishes architecture, not Voynich channel membership or meaning gold.
design.related: Near GDT213 and GDT247 ownership work, but targets argument arity and channel transition rather than proximity ownership or label identity.

source_evidence.quote:
Ashmole 399 supplies the strongest readable precedent so far for q13's mixed
page architecture, but not for its content or exact topology. A medieval
medical page can combine an abstract connected system, short inscriptions
owned by individual components, one embedded humanlike figure, and dense
longer practical text. Another abstract-system page in the same manuscript
uses predominantly continuous prose instead, showing that caption and prose
layouts can vary within one technical codex.
